chunks: "A wafer is a thin, round disc of extremely pure single-crystal silicon that serves as the base on which chips are built.
Think of it as the canvas for manufacturing: instead of making chips one at a time, a fab builds hundreds or thousands of identical dies across the wafer at once, then cuts them apart.
It's made by melting very pure silicon and slowly pulling a seed crystal out of the melt, the Czochralski process, which grows a long cylindrical single crystal called an ingot.
The ingot is sliced into discs, which are ground, etched and polished until they're flat to nanometre-scale roughness.
The standard size for modern leading-edge fabs is 300 millimetres across, about 775 micrometres thick, with a small notch that marks the crystal orientation.
Older and specialty fabs use 200 or 150 millimetre wafers.
Wafers are round because of how the crystal is grown, and bigger wafers are better economically: a 300 millimetre wafer has 2.
25 times the area of a 200 millimetre one, so the processing cost is spread over more dies.
For example, a 100 square millimetre die gives roughly 640 candidate dies on a 300 mm wafer, minus some loss at the edges, and then yield determines how many are good.
So the wafer is the substrate, a die is one chip cut from it, and the package is what the die ends up in."
